  cellular networks hold seconds of data in operator
  buffers. Delay-based algorithms (Vegas, Westwood)
  and hybrids (Compound TCP) sought other signals.
  Google's BBR, deployed in 2016, abandoned inference
  entirely: it measures the bottleneck bandwidth and
  minimum RTT directly, then paces packets to fill
  exactly the bandwidth-delay product without building
   queues. On lossy and long-delay paths BBR is
  transformative, and it now carries much of Google's
  and Netflix's traffic — though early versions were
  unfair to CUBIC on shared bottlenecks, a problem the
   BBRv2/v3 line explicitly targets.

  The latest shift is where the algorithm lives. QUIC
  implements congestion control in userspace, so
  improvements ship with applications instead of
  waiting on kernel releases. Specialized regimes have
   their own controllers — DCQCN for RDMA datacenters,
   Swift and Copa for tail latency, tuned profiles for
   5G.

  Four decades on, the skeleton is unchanged: probe
  gently, back off multiplicatively, share fairly.
  What evolved is everything around that skeleton —
  what counts as congestion evidence, how fast
  capacity is probed, and where the algorithm runs.

  DONE
